subject: zoology_2
question_text: Describe male reproductive system of a man. Draw a labelled diagram of it.

mark_split.label: The six parts and the testes

verification.note: Sourced from 'My Baby Bullet-Q — Senior Inter Zoology' (Star-Q Pass Track Series, Sri Publishers, 2022), book pp.18-19, LAQ 5. The printed exam years are the book's claim, reproduced here as appearances. Zoology-II holds only ONE source book in the corpus, so the two-book union check is structurally impossible for this card; 'not checked' does NOT mean 'checked and clean'. The mark split is our reading of the question and is a claim until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it.

steps.label: The six parts and the testes
steps.why: Sperm will not develop at body temperature, so the testes hang outside the abdomen where it is a few degrees cooler.
common_mistakes: Leaving out why the testes lie outside. That is the marked reason.
steps.memory_tip: Outside the body because sperm need it cooler.
steps.margin_note: Six parts listed, then the testis.
lines: The male reproductive system has 6 parts:
testes, epididymis, vasa deferentia,
urethra, penis and accessory glands.
The testes are a pair of oval pinkish male
primary sex organs.
They hang outside the abdominal cavity in a
pouch called the scrotum, because sperms do
not develop at body temperature.
The scrotum joins the abdominal cavity
through the inguinal canal, and the testis
is held inside it by the gubernaculum.

steps.label: Inside the testis
steps.why: Packing 250 lobules of coiled tubules into one small organ is what gives the enormous surface needed to make sperm continuously.
common_mistakes: Giving one seminiferous tubule per testis. Each lobule holds two or three.
steps.memory_tip: 250 lobules, two or three coiled tubules in each.
steps.margin_note: The numbers are marked. Write them.
lines: The spermatic cord is formed by the blood
vessels, nerve and vas deferens. It runs
from the abdomen to each testis through the
inguinal canal.
The tunica albuginea projects inside the
testis as septa. There are about 250
testicular lobules in each testis.
Each lobule holds two or three highly
coiled seminiferous tubules.

steps.label: Sertoli and Leydig cells
steps.why: One cell type feeds the developing sperm inside the tubule while the other makes the hormone outside it, so the two jobs never interfere.
common_mistakes: Giving Sertoli cells the hormone job. Leydig cells make testosterone.
Placing Leydig cells inside the tubules. They lie between them.
steps.memory_tip: Sertoli cells feed the sperm inside; Leydig cells make testosterone outside.
steps.margin_note: Say where each cell sits as well as what it does.
lines: Each seminiferous tubule has germinal
epithelium and Sertoli cells.
The germinal epithelium produces sperms and
the Sertoli cells nourish them.
The regions outside the seminiferous
tubules are the interstitial spaces, which
contain Leydig cells.
Leydig cells make the male hormone
testosterone, an androgen, which controls
the secondary sexual characters and
spermatogenesis.

steps.label: Epididymis
steps.why: Sperm leaving the testis cannot yet swim, so they are held in the epididymis until they mature.
common_mistakes: Writing that sperm are made in the epididymis. They mature and are stored there.
Naming only two of its three regions.
steps.memory_tip: Caput, corpus, cauda — head, body, tail.
steps.margin_note: Name the path from the tubules to the epididymis.
lines: The seminiferous tubules open into the rete
testis, which opens into the vasa
efferentia, which open into the epididymis.
It is a narrow tightly coiled tube along
the posterior surface of each testis.
It gives space for the maturation and
storage of sperms.
It has three regions: caput epididymis,
corpus epididymis and cauda epididymis.

steps.label: Vasa deferentia and urethra
steps.why: The urethra is shared by two systems, which is why it is called the urinogenital duct in the male.
common_mistakes: Giving the male a separate duct for urine and semen. There is one.
Leaving out where the vas deferens opens.
steps.memory_tip: One tube for two jobs: the urinogenital duct.
steps.margin_note: Follow the tube: epididymis, abdomen, prostate, urethra.
lines: Each is a long narrow muscular tube. It
starts at the tail of the epididymis,
passes through the inguinal canal into the
abdomen and loops over the urinary bladder.
The two ducts open into the urethra at the
centre of the prostate gland.
The urethra starts from the urinary bladder
and runs through the penis to its external
opening, the urethral meatus.
It is the shared terminal duct of the
reproductive and urinary systems, so it is
called the urinogenital duct of man.

steps.label: Penis
steps.why: Three columns of spongy tissue fill with blood, which is what makes the organ stiff enough to deliver sperm.
common_mistakes: Naming two columns. There are three.
Leaving out the term intromittent organ.
steps.memory_tip: Two corpora cavernosa above, one corpus spongiosum below.
steps.margin_note: Name the three columns and the covering.
lines: The penis serves as a urinal duct. It is
the intromittent organ that carries
spermatozoa to the vagina of the female.
It has three columns of tissue: two upper
corpora cavernosa and one ventral corpus
spongiosum.
The enlarged terminal part is the glans
penis, covered by loose skin called the
prepuce or foreskin.
The special tissue of the three columns
helps the penis to become erect.

steps.label: Accessory glands
steps.why: Each gland adds something the sperm needs: fuel, activation, and an alkaline fluid to protect them from acid.
common_mistakes: Naming two glands. There are three.
Leaving out fructose, which is the sperm's fuel.
steps.memory_tip: Seminal vesicle feeds, prostate activates, bulbourethral lubricates.
steps.margin_note: Give the percentage each contributes. Those figures are marked.
lines: Seminal vesicles are a pair of simple
tubular glands below the urinary bladder.
Each opens into its own vas deferens.
Their secretion is 60% of the seminal
fluid. It is alkaline and viscous, and its
fructose is the main energy source of the
sperm.
The prostate gland lies below the urinary
bladder and gives 15 to 30% of the seminal
fluid. Its slightly acid secretion
activates the sperms and feeds them.
Bulbourethral glands lie below the prostate
and add an alkaline fluid during
ejaculation, which lubricates the urethra.

steps.label: Diagram — male reproductive system
steps.why: The diagram shows the one thing the description cannot: that the vas deferens loops up and over the bladder before reaching the urethra.
common_mistakes: Drawing the vas deferens straight to the urethra. It loops over the bladder.
Leaving out the three accessory glands.
steps.memory_tip: Testis, epididymis, up and over the bladder, down the urethra.
steps.margin_note: Label at least ten parts, including all three glands.

elements.caption: Step 1 — the urinary bladder and the ureters
Step 2 — the seminal vesicles and the prostate
Step 3 — the urethra and the penis
Step 4 — the testis, epididymis and vas deferens

insider_note: The most repeated 8-mark question in the paper — nine printed appearances. The scrotum question ('why outside the body?') is worth one line and is often the difference between a good answer and a full one.
